topic: Causes of inflation: demand-pull (and bottleneck) vs cost-push, told with one bread shop, then the Monetarist view that both need more money in people's hands

concepts.name: inflation = rise in the general price level
demand-pull: more buyers for the same bread, price 50 -> 65
rule: demand-pull works whenever demand exceeds supply
bottleneck (structural) inflation: supply drops, demand unchanged
cost-push: input costs rise, demand and supply unchanged, price 50 -> 55
concepts.prereq_recalled: the same bread shop; factory input costs (labour, raw material)

concepts.name: Monetarist view of demand-pull: demand rises only with more purchasing power
Monetarist view of cost-push: higher prices last only if buyers have extra money, so cost-push is not independent

book_understanding.teaching_order: A textbook defines demand-pull and cost-push with a formula-like sentence each and a diagram of shifting curves. The video names the two causes and the two schools up front, then teaches everything with one tiny market (one bread shop, two packets, two buyers at 50 rupees) and changes one thing at a time: more buyers, then fewer packets, then a costlier factory behind the shop. Each time the term is given only after the price has visibly moved. The second school is taught last, as a frame that sits under the first school's whole tree and claims one cause (more money in people's hands) under both branches.
book_understanding.breakdown_rule: Keep one small market fixed and change one node at a time (demand, supply, cost); each change that moves the price is one teachable cause, named after it is seen.

opening.what: Last video: a rise in the general price level is inflation. But why does the price level rise at all? Today: the causes.

examples.what: One bread shop in a locality with two packets a day at 50 rupees, and two buyers ready to pay 50.
examples.carries: a balanced market as the base scene for all three causes

examples.what: More people want bread; the shopkeeper tries 65 and two of the crowd pay it.
The shop now has one packet while the same two buyers remain; one pays more (60 on screen).
If the government suddenly changes a policy, a disaster hits, or factories lack infrastructure support, supply drops.
The store buys from a factory whose labour and raw-material costs rise; the higher cost is passed down to the shelf price (55 on screen).
Buyers who need bread cut back on other things to pay the higher price.

closing.what: One-line recap of the causes and both schools, then a pointer to WPI and CPI in the next video and a playlist plug.

narration.density: About 13 terms (inflation, general price level, cost-push, demand-pull, Keynesian school, Monetarist school, demand, supply, bottleneck inflation, structural inflation, input cost, inflation tax, purchasing power) in about 7.4 minutes, under 2 per minute. Comfortable and slow-feeling: the bread example takes most of the time; the Monetarist part is compressed into the last minute and a half of talk over text boxes.

talmel_summary: For the Keynesian part the picture shows the step: one store - price - demand template where buyers multiply, prices are struck and rewritten, crosses fall under buyers who cannot pay, a packet disappears, and a factory is joined in front, so each cause is one visible change on the same scene. The picture usually leads by 1-5 s, and in two places it shows numbers the voice never says (60, 55) or shows 65 nine seconds early. The Monetarist part is four text boxes inside a frame; only the loop lines from one bar to both branches carry the idea visually. Note: the tile text in talmel/E15/tiles.json comes from a failed transcript, so lead and gist here use a re-transcript (English narration).

voice.notes: Narration is in English, unlike the other Hindi videos of this channel (detected English with 0.995 confidence; the batch transcript forced Hindi and failed after 30 s). About 176 words per minute, calm, explanatory, with frequent 'basically', 'suppose', 'let's assume', 'so we saw that'. Numbers read as '50 rupees', '65 rupees'. Conclusions are restated twice ('no change in demand or supply... the changes in prices have occurred only because of the increase in costs'). No humour; even tone throughout. One recognition slip ('50 euros') should read 50 rupees.

game_ideas.player_does: Runs the one bread shop: each day an event card hits (more buyers arrive, a packet is lost, the factory raises its price), the learner sets the day's price and then tags the cause as demand-pull, bottleneck or cost-push.
game_ideas.process_happens: Buyers with 'ready to pay' tags line up; at the learner's price the packets move to the buyers who can pay and crosses fall under the rest; the node that changed (demand, supply, cost) lights up on the supply - price - demand line.
game_ideas.win: Sell out every day without losing money and tag every cause correctly.
game_ideas.lose: Too low a price leaves a long queue and an empty shelf; too high leaves bread unsold; a wrong tag replays the day highlighting the node that really changed.

game_ideas.player_does: Sorts news cards (festival crowds rush the market, a flood ruins the wheat crop, bakery wages rise, a sudden ban on a raw material, a cash bonus for every family) into demand-pull, bottleneck (structural) and cost-push.
game_ideas.process_happens: Each card, when dropped, plays on the bread-shop scene: buyers multiply, packets vanish, or the factory's cost chip rises, and the price tag moves.
game_ideas.win: All cards placed with the matching scene change.
game_ideas.lose: Putting the flood under cost-push shows that only the shelf emptied while the factory cost stayed the same, with a nudge to look at the supply node.

game_ideas.player_does: Controls how much money is in the two buyers' wallets while the factory raises its cost and the shopkeeper tries 55.
game_ideas.process_happens: With no extra money the buyers refuse 55 and bread sits unsold until the price falls back; with fuller wallets 55 sticks; adding money with no cost change also pulls the price up.
game_ideas.win: Show a price rise that lasts, and notice it lasts only when wallets grow.
game_ideas.lose: Raising cost alone shows the price spike and fall back, with the Monetarist note 'cost-push is not independent'.
game_ideas.concept: Monetarist view: inflation needs more money in people's hands

notes_questions.q: Inflation kya hai aur iske do kaaran kaun se hain?
Bread shop ke example se demand-pull inflation samjhaiye (50 se 65 kaise hua?).
Bottleneck ya structural inflation kab hota hai? Teen udaharan dijiye.
Cost-push inflation mein demand aur supply badalte hain kya? Phir price kyon badhta hai?
Teeno cases mein kya badla: demand, supply ya cost? Table banaiye.

Monetarist kyon kehte hain ki cost-push inflation independent theory nahi hai?

checks_learned: Every number on screen must be spoken (60 and 55 appear only on screen).
A number should not appear more than about 3 s before the voice reaches it (65 leads by about 9 s).
When the voice says something is unchanged (demand, supply in cost-push), the screen should mark it unchanged; E15 does this only for the bottleneck case.
Comparing causes should reuse one scene and mark only the node that changed (E15 does this; enforce it).
A stretch of more than about 60 s with only text boxes (the Monetarist view) should be flagged for a picture.
A transcript where one token repeats many times is a failed transcript: re-run with language detection before any timing check (E15's narration was English, forced Hindi produced loops).
If a case is named as a subtype of two things (bottleneck from a supply drop, yet 'still demand-pull'), the lesson must say plainly how both hold.

teaching_best.why: The crowd grows, the price is struck and rewritten, crosses fall under buyers who cannot pay and the packets go to the few who can: demand-pull seen before it is named.
The same scene with one packet removed shows exactly what changed; the 'but actually' turn then reframes it as bottleneck inflation.
A factory joined in front of the same template, with the voice stating demand and supply unchanged, isolates cost as the only cause.
Names who bears cost-push: buyers cut back on other things to pay the higher price.
The Monetarist frame sits under the whole Keynesian tree and loops up to both branches: one cause under two names.

teaching_weak.why: 65 appears about 9 s before it is spoken; 60 and 55 are never spoken.
The Monetarist argument is text boxes; no wallets or money flow are shown, though the whole claim is about money in hands.
'Raised by hit and trial' is said with no picture of the price being tried step by step.
Bottleneck is called structural and yet 'still demand-pull' without reconciling the two labels.
The two schools are introduced as pills with dates about 5 minutes before the second one is used.
